program_note:
In a fugue, a melody is chased by another statement of that same melody—the first voice thus fleeing from the second.  Typically, that first pair of voices will be joined by another voice or pair of voices, leading to a brief moment of repose (a cadence).  Beyond that, there is little common to all fugues from all eras, or even to all fugues by a single composer (or even just of the 48 fugues in J.S. Bach’s Well-Tempered Clavier).  The relationship of an introductory prelude to the fugue itself is even less well established.  In this set of preludes and fugues, the preludes serve primarily to introduce and establish the mode used in the two pieces, although material from some of the preludes are also used in their respective fugues as respites (episodes) from the main fugal melody.
The thirteen Preludes and Fugues are written in a total of seven different “modes,” or scale patterns, nearly all of which were created for this set.  Four pairs work with the same mode (numbers 1 & 8, 3 & 10, 5 & 11, and 6 & 12), while numbers 2, 4, & 9 use the same mode.  Numbers 7 and 13 each use a unique mode; only number 13 uses a pre-existing mode.
Numbers 7 and 13 are also unusual in that the Prelude flows into and continues during the Fugue (creating an accompanied fugue).  The number of voices in these two fugues are also unique in the set:  only two voices in number 7, and five in number 13.  Most of the other Fugues are either for three or four voices (Fugue 2 is a double fugue, each with two voices, for a total of four—hence “4-in-2”—while Fugue 9 has many voices embedded recursively in the three main voices).
Each Prelude and Fugue is dedicated to a composer or musician who has had an influence on my music, and for a pianist whom I have admired.  Number 13 is again unique in this regard:  written toward the end of a particularly difficult and tumultuous year in the United States, it is dedicated “To a Convalescing Nation,” in the hope that it will speedily recover from the malaise that was 2020.  The Lydian mode, used in this pair of pieces, is associated with convalescing and healing (see, for instance, Beethoven’s String Quartet No.15, Op.132, iii).  Because number 13 runs attacca from the previous pair, they are both written for the same pianist.
The title “Expanded Universe” refers, first, to the expansion to thirteen preludes and fugues from an earlier set of ten (number 13 is the “bonus” of this baker’s dozen).  Second, each mode created for this set expands the notion of “scale,” both in terms of overall size (from an octave to anywhere from one-and-a-half to six octaves) and in terms of the intervals used (from whole and half steps to intervals as large as perfect fourths).
The duration of the entire set is just under 78 minutes, as shown below.  There is no need to perform all of the set together.
